chapter_theme: The Lord is within, so every outward search misses him: Sivavakkiyar mocks pilgrimage, bathing, counted japa, darbha-grass puja, spittle rules and the planted stone, and against them sets the light within, the eight and two, the one letter, the nine gates and the gate of knowledge. Several verses end in the refrain சிவாயமே, and a few are plain prayers and confessions of the 'I' destroyed in the ocean of silence.
structure_note: The chapter alternates: attacks on outward practice (1439 to 1444, 1448, 1456 to 1458) and cipher verses on the inner path (1449 to 1454), with prayers and first-person verses between (1445 to 1447, 1455, 1459) and a close on impermanence (1461 to 1463).

1439.reading: With a thieving heart still in you, you recite transcendent knowledge; when the deceit within is cut away, do you not see that this itself is the way? If you can polish the heart daily and draw near the light, clear knowledge has excelled within you: Sivaayame.
1439.nuance: கள்ளம் (deceit, theft) is the one fault named, and its removal is called the கதி, the way or goal, itself. The verse makes knowledge a result of cleaning the heart, not of reciting.

1440.reading: Wanting to see, you climb seas and mountains; is that not egoism, people without understanding? If you wish it and hold the Lord's feet within the true body, the soul standing as the pillar becomes Siva itself.
1440.nuance: ஆணவம் is the Siddhanta name for the root impurity of self-assertion, and the verse calls pilgrimage itself an act of it. தாணு (pillar, Sthanu) is a name of Siva and here the soul standing firm; the last line says the jiva becomes Siva, stated flatly.

1441.reading: If you mark and look within yourselves, as your own nature, at the immeasurable light that is at once atom and universe, that is release; muttering and counting on your fingers, in a confusion from which there is no return, out of lack of resolve you keep on doing puja.
1441.nuance: அணுவினோடு அகண்டம் (with the atom, the undivided whole) is the Siddhar formula for the light as both smallest and largest. விரலை எண்ணி (counting on the fingers) is counted japa, and துணிவிலாத படியினால் makes repetition a failure of nerve.

1442.reading: Poor ones who shrink saying 'spittle, spittle': was it not from base spittle that the pure body itself came? Is not the honey the bee's spittle, and the flower too? Even the milk drawn with the hand on the cow's teat is spittle.
1442.nuance: Each example is a thing the pollution-keeper eats: honey, milk, and the body itself (from semen, the துச்சில் or base fluid). The verse does not argue that pollution is harmless but that the rule cannot be kept consistently.

1443.reading: Wicked ones who run about seeking 'the holy water, the linga, the image': make clear the soul standing within as the holy-water linga; if you can see the holy-water linga clearly within you, the holy-water linga itself is what has excelled as That: Sivaayame.
1443.nuance: தீர்த்தலிங்கம் repeats as the first word of all four lines, shifting from the thing sought outside to the soul within and then to Siva. The compound may mean a linga bathed in sacred water or a linga at a sacred ford.

1444.reading: Like keeping a goat, dividing it and sitting down; spreading the sought-for copper firmly; while the Lord you seek is within us, what is this puja of throwing darbha grass, what puja, what puja?
1444.nuance: Line 1 may describe animal sacrifice (ஆடு கொண்டு கூறு செய்து, taking a goat and cutting it in portions) and line 2 the copper vessel or image laid out for rites; both are tentative. The thrice-repeated பூசை என்ன is clear enough: the rite is pointless while the Lord is within.

1445.reading: Lord who does not forget me even for a moment, One, God, King of kings of kings: can I stay without you even a moment? Help me, Lord, that your name be on my tongue.
1445.nuance: A plain prayer with no polemic. The one request is for the name on the tongue, which sits beside the chapter's mockery of muttered mantra and shows the difference the poet draws between them: remembering versus counting.

1446.reading: With the limitless light burning as one, the mighty Full Radiance becoming sole enjoyment, pressing good joy into the ocean of silence, I ate the nectar none can seek, and stood on that day with 'I' destroyed.
1446.nuance: நான் அழிந்து (I destroyed) is the verse's end-point, and மோனசாகரம் (ocean of silence) the medium. The verse is in the past tense as testimony, which is rare in the chapter's imperatives and questions.

1447.reading: If you can gladly see within yourselves, showing the flesh, the undivided light that has become as it has: you can rule this fleshly body, rule the burden of the world, rule the forest land too, by the oath of the Lord of colours.
1447.nuance: The three ஆளலாம் promise mastery of body, world and a third realm (கானநாடு, forest land, perhaps for வானநாடு, the sky). ஊனைகாட்டி (showing the flesh) is unclear. The verse is the chapter's only promise of power, and it is conditional on inner seeing.

1448.reading: Daily polishing the bell, going into the long corner to sit, muttering and wailing with eyes closed, what is the use? However many count, are eight and two not ten? Does this suit the Father, people without understanding?
1448.nuance: எட்டிரண்டும் பத்தலோ (are eight and two not ten?) is a cipher: in Tamil numerals ௮ (eight) and ௨ (two) look like the letters அ and உ, so 'eight and two' names the pranava letters, and 'ten' may then be their union. The plain sense is only that counting cannot change what is.

1449.reading: If you can regard within yourselves, in due measure, the god who became the linga when eight and two joined, you can cross the dark sea of hard birth, and you will stay joined with the light you love: see.
1449.nuance: The 'eight and two' of 1448 now form the linga: on the numeral reading, அ and உ (the sun and moon, or the two breaths, in the Siddhars' usage) joined make the inner linga. கருங்கடல் (dark sea) is the sea of births.

1450.reading: The true mantra stays in the light; the cool mantra has taken shape and become form; the white mantra has ripened and become ash; the true mantra is that one alone: Sivaayame.
1450.nuance: Three mantras, true, cool and white, are hard to fix: they may be the mantra as light, as embodied form and as the sacred ash, with the refrain சிவாயமே naming the one that matters. The verse ranks and then collapses them.

1451.reading: At the carpenter's gate, above the crown, as a thousand places; three lights and three-two, the fire-flame that blazed up; where did it grow and stand as the diamond? And how did this flame and the senses become one?
1451.nuance: A cipher verse: the thousand places at the crown are the thousand-petalled centre as tradition reads it, the three lights sun, moon and fire, மூவிரண்டு perhaps the six centres, and வச்சிரம் (diamond, vajra) the hardened state. தச்சுவாயில் (carpenter's gate) is unexplained. The verse asks rather than tells.

1452.reading: The nine strong gates, the gate that is shut and refused, the five gates that speak, and what stood swelling to speak: open the good gate, go through the gate of knowledge, and once the boundary gate is seen there is no more birth.
1452.nuance: The nine gates are the body's openings; the shut tenth gate is, in yogic tradition, the opening at the crown, and the five that speak the senses. The verse sets a sequence of gates ending at the எல்லைவாசல், the boundary gate, beyond which birth ceases.

1453.reading: All the honey that came with the bee and the flower's scents is eaten and subsides within; in that manner, reciting with the root of the linga, if you can see and see and make thought subside at the root, the strong deeds taken on of old fly away: Sivaayame.
1453.nuance: The honey drawn in and settled is the figure for attention drawn to the root (வேர்); லிங்க மூலம் may be the root centre or the base of the inner linga. The verse's claim is that old deeds leave when thought settles there.

1454.reading: In the one letter as the linga, within that letter which you recite, you do not know the truth that one letter moves; the light that sprouted as three from the three letters, the four letters have uttered on the tongue: Sivaayame.
1454.nuance: One, three and four letters: the one is usually Om, the three its parts அ உ ம் as the three gods (மூவராய்), and the four may be சிவாய without the ந-ம. The verse's charge is that reciters do not know what moves inside the letter they recite.

1455.reading: Sinners who grieved saying 'far, far, far, the distance that rose and rose, burden, burden, burden': if you can keep thinking of him time after time, moment by moment, even that far, far, far distance can be joined.
1455.nuance: The verse is built on tripled words (தூர, பார, நேர), and its argument is that distance from the Lord is a matter of attention: continuous remembrance (நினைந்திருக்க) closes it. It answers the pilgrims of 1440, who tried to close the distance by travel.

1456.reading: Wearing earrings you plunge into every tank; like frogs you never scrape the dirt from the mind; if you could keep the bearer of the skull in your mind, you could live bowed to by ancient Mal and Ayan.
1456.nuance: The frog lives in water and stays slimy, which is the whole argument against bathing as purification. மண்டை ஏந்து கையர் (he who bears the skull in hand) is Siva as the beggar; the promise is to be worshipped by Vishnu and Brahma.

1457.reading: As one builds a nest and lays eggs and sits; the goat that bore two kids dances in the hall; you human cattle who keep cows and eat butter: once the house is found, the open space too will be seen.
1457.nuance: A cipher verse. ஆடு (goat) also means 'dance', and the goat with two kids dancing in the hall (அம்பலம்) may encode the Dancer with his two, perhaps the two letters or the two breaths; மானிடப் பசுக்கள் (human cattle) plays on pasu as beast and bound soul. வீடு is both house and release, and வெட்டவெளி the open space of the formless.

1458.reading: Calling a planted stone a god, laying four flowers on it, circling it and muttering, what mantra is this? Will the planted stone speak while the Lord is within? Does the fired pot or the ladle know the taste of the curry?
1458.nuance: The best-known of Sivavakkiyar's verses. The pot and ladle argument is that a vessel is not the thing it holds; the verse's premise, stated in line 3, is that the Lord is within the worshipper, not that there is no Lord.

1459.reading: Not I, not you, not the Lord, I declare; not in the sky, not the light; the light is within us. When I and you have become alike, can it still be sought and seen? Taana taana tantaana taatanaana taananaa.
1459.nuance: The denials remove every term, including the Lord, and leave only a light within; the question of line 3 may mean that once seeker and sought are alike there is no seeking. The last line is drum syllables, a filler or a refusal to say more.

1460.reading: What stands in the middle, neither good nor bad, is one thing; once what is called good has gone and stood as good, if one says 'not good, bad', it becomes bad; therefore stand seeking what is good and say the name.
1460.nuance: The verse says value follows naming: calling a thing bad makes it so. Its conclusion is practical, not sceptical: since names shape things, hold to the good one and say the Lord's name.

1461.reading: In the loveless forest where ghouls gather and eat corpses, where dogs surround him and he dances, what is the life of Namban? If you seek, wishing to be rid of the desire that rises with mothers' milk, look within yourselves at how you whirl, struck by diseases.
1461.nuance: Siva as the cremation-ground dancer is the opening image; the question ஏதடா may be scorn or wonder. தாய்கள் பால் உதிக்கும் இச்சை is desire that begins at the breast, which is the desire for birth itself. How the two halves join is unclear.

1462.reading: A body that rots and becomes a spring of filth if the salt is removed: can you hold desire for it? Tell me, O mind, witless, false, honourless rogue, and listen: the feet of the one with the matchless red matted locks are the truth.
1462.nuance: உப்பை நீக்கில் (if the salt is removed) treats the body as preserved meat; the salt may be the breath or life. The verse is addressed to the poet's own mind, not to others, and ends with the one thing called true.

1463.reading: All that is born dies; foolish people do not understand, and rejoice as if there were no dying, talk in hints of 'our property and yours' and wander about; what is this guise they have put on? When the filled body perishes, will there be love then, Lord?
1463.nuance: கொண்ட கோலம் (the guise taken on) applies the chapter's language of false garb to ordinary householders, whose pretence is that they will not die. The last line asks whether the love bound to property survives the body.

links.note: The Kural asks what an appearance high as the sky can do if the heart sinks into a known fault; Sivavakkiyar asks what reciting transcendent knowledge does while a thieving heart remains. Both make the inner fault cancel the outward height.

Tirumular says there are many holy waters within the heart and those who do not bathe there wander over hollow and height; Sivavakkiyar says those who climb seas and mountains to see the Lord act from ego, when his feet can be held within. Both turn the pilgrim's road inward.

Both verses argue from spittle: 1423 that the mantra itself is spittle from the mouth, 1442 that honey, milk and the body are spittle too. Together they make the pollution rule self-defeating from two sides, what the ritualist utters and what he eats.

Tirumular makes the heart the temple and, for those clear through and through, the soul the Sivalinga; Sivavakkiyar tells those who run after holy water, linga and image to see the soul within as the linga. Both use the same identification and the same condition of clarity (தெளிவு).

The Kural says the one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' enters a world above the gods'; Sivavakkiyar reports the day he stood with 'I' destroyed in the ocean of silence. The Kural's is an ethic of renunciation, the Siddhar's an experience, but the thing removed is the same.

Tirumular says there is no need to cry out once the meaning is grasped and no need of sounded chant once samadhi is in hand; Sivavakkiyar asks what use polishing bells, sitting in a corner and wailing with closed eyes can be. Both dismiss the noise of practice once its point is seen.

Both use the cipher 'eight and two' (எட்டும் இரண்டும்): Tirumular says those who do not know the eight and two miss the step of the Siddhanta path, Sivavakkiyar says the god became the linga when eight and two joined. Neither explains it; the shared figure, read as the letters அ and உ, ties the two texts.

Tirumular says that if one door is closed inside the bag of the body, light shines within and the temple is lit; Sivavakkiyar lists the nine gates and the shut gate and says that going through the gate of knowledge to the boundary gate ends birth. Both make the body's openings the yogic path.

Tirumular says that by one letter he became everything, by two he joined as two and by three letters the light springs up; Sivavakkiyar speaks of the one letter that moves, the three letters from which the light sprouted as three, and the four letters on the tongue. The counting of letters as stages of the light is shared.

Both use the frog that stays slimy in water: the Naladiyar for readers of flawless books who never gain discernment, Sivavakkiyar for bathers who never scrape the dirt from the mind. The image makes the same point in two domains, that immersion does not clean.
Tirumular ranks those who know only bathing lowest and says they cannot join him; Sivavakkiyar's tank-bathers never clean the mind. Both put bathing below inner clarity.

Both use the ladle that cannot taste what it stirs: the Naladiyar for the fool who mocks teaching he cannot savour, Sivavakkiyar for the stone and pot that cannot know the Lord they are made to hold. The same kitchen image serves ethics in one and the critique of idols in the other.

Tirumular lists lamps, flowers, bell and the bathing of the image and calls the work of the temple the servant's path (சரியை); Sivavakkiyar asks what mantra it is that circles a planted stone with four flowers, since the stone will not speak. The conflict holds if Sivavakkiyar denies temple rites any place; it eases if he mocks only those who stop there, since Tirumular too ranks சரியை lowest.

Arunagirinathar describes the body as filth wrapped in skin, a hut of nine gates perishing faster than a bubble, and regrets desiring it; Sivavakkiyar says the body rots without its salt and asks his mind how it can desire it. Both set contempt for the body against attachment, and both end at the Lord's feet.

The Naladiyar scorns those who see that life may leave in a blink and still do no good; Sivavakkiyar scorns those who know all that is born dies and still talk of 'our property and yours' as if deathless. Both treat denial of death as the root folly of householders.

source_issues: 1459 line 4 is drum syllables (தானதான தந்தான தாதனான தானனா), not a verse line; it may be a singer's filler that entered the text or a lost line's replacement.
1444 lines 1 and 2 (ஆடுகொண்டு கூறுசெய்து, தேடுகின்ற செம்பினைத் திடப்படப் பரப்பியே) are hard to construe and may be corrupt.
1447 line 4 கானநாடும் may be a corruption of வானநாடும்.
